questions: What is the exact definition of "modulo" in the output specification - what modulus should be used?
How should the case be handled when no good sequences exist - should we output 0 or is at least one guaranteed?
Are intermediate calculations allowed to overflow, or must they be performed modulo some value throughout?
Is the gcd condition strictly necessary for a sequence to be considered good, or is it just an additional constraint?
What is the precise mathematical domain for the values in sequence S - must they be positive integers or could they be any positive rationals?
How should ties or equivalent sequences be handled in the summation - are they counted multiple times or once?
Is there a guarantee that coprime integers P and Q satisfying the equation are unique for each ratio?
Should the empty product (when N=0) be considered as contributing 1 to the sum, or is N≥2 always guaranteed?
answers: Not guaranteed to exist; if no good sequence exists, output 0.
Not specified; a standard approach is to reduce intermediate values modulo 998244353 throughout to avoid overflow.
Yes, the gcd condition is part of the definition of a good sequence, not optional.
S consists only of positive integers, as stated.
Not applicable; each distinct good sequence is a distinct tuple and contributes its score once.
Yes, the reduced coprime P,Q representation of any ratio is unique by definition.
Not applicable; N is guaranteed to be at least 2.

For a positive rational number x, define f(x) as follows:
Express x as $\dfrac{P}{Q}$ using coprime positive integers P and Q. f(x) is defined as the value P\times Q.
You are given a positive integer N and a sequence A=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_{N-1}) of positive integers of length N-1.
We call a sequence S=(S_1,S_2,\dots,S_N) of positive integers of length N a good sequence if it satisfies all of the following conditions:
- For every integer i with 1\leq i\leq N-1, it holds that f$\left(\dfrac{S_i}{S_{i+1}}\right)$=A_i.
- $\gcd(S_1,S_2,\dots,S_N)$=1.
